lesson.title: Walking Through Both Sides: Key-Value Pairs
lesson.summary: The .keys(), .values(), and .items() methods let you work with a dictionary's keys, values, or key-value pairs together, most often by looping over them.
lesson.body:
Dictionaries introduced the key-value pair as the basic unit a dictionary is built from, each key mapped to one value. So far, individual pairs have been accessed one at a time using square brackets, student["name"]. Often, though, you want to work through every pair in a dictionary at once, and Python provides three methods built specifically for that.

.keys() returns all the keys in a dictionary, .values() returns all the values, and .items() returns every key-value pair together, each pair given to you as a tuple of (key, value). All three are typically looped over directly with a for statement, and because dictionaries preserve insertion order since Python 3.7, looping over any of them visits entries in the exact order they were added to the dictionary.

prices = {"apple": 0.50, "bread": 3.25, "milk": 2.75}

for item, cost in prices.items():
    print(f"{item}: ${cost:.2f}")

This loop prints three lines, in insertion order:
apple: $0.50
bread: $3.25
milk: $2.75

Each pass through the loop unpacks one (key, value) tuple from .items() into the two loop variables item and cost, the same kind of tuple unpacking used elsewhere when working with tuples. If you only need the keys or only need the values, list(prices.keys()) gives ['apple', 'bread', 'milk'] and list(prices.values()) gives [0.5, 3.25, 2.75].

One subtlety worth knowing: .keys(), .values(), and .items() don't return plain lists, they return special view objects that stay connected to the dictionary. If the dictionary changes after you grab a view, the view reflects that change automatically the next time you look at it, without needing to call the method again. This is different from taking a fixed snapshot, and it's usually exactly what you want, since it means a loop over prices.items() will always reflect the dictionary's current contents rather than some outdated copy.
